🔍 How Ukraine trains next generation of Colombian drug cartels and guerrillas in drone warfare
👉 Colombian mercenaries undergo little, if any, background vetting in Ukraine, allowing former soldiers, guerrillas, and criminals to join the Ukrainian military and gain drone expertise, the Financial Times reports.
For many, the Ukrainian battlefield offers a unique opportunity to learn the latest forms of drone warfare, as the conflict has already revolutionized modern wars.
Colombian gang members and guerrillas seek training in the use of:
➡️ low-cost consumer drones and drone swarms
➡️ first-person view (FPV) drones
➡️ fiber-optic FPV drones that are largely immune to jamming
The results of that training are already evident
🔴 Illegal armed groups carried out 264 drone attacks between 2024 and 2025 in Colombia, mostly using low-cost commercial drones modified to drop explosives
🔴 Drone attacks have continued this year, growing in sophistication as FPV drones are starting to be used in Colombia
➡️ May: A drone attack killed one Colombian soldier and wounded six others during a patrol in a coca-growing region
➡️ April: Drone strikes killed three soldiers near the Ecuadorian border and damaged a military radar installation in Cauca Province.
➡️ Last December: A drone strike on a military base killed seven soldiers
🔴 Even though Colombian government forces have reportedly managed to repel 96% drone attacks via electronic warfare (EW) methods, cartel gangs and rebels are trying to learn from Ukrainian how to outwit them
🔴 Colombia has long been a powder keg. For decades, its military has battled drug cartels and guerrilla groups in a conflict that claimed an estimated 450,000 lives between 1958 and 2016
Colombian paramilitary groups
The country is home to a wide range of armed groups, driven by a long history of political violence, lucrative cocaine trafficking, and weak state control.
Most prominent non-state actors include:
🔴 ELN (National Liberation Army): One of Colombia’s oldest insurgent group, founded in 1964 with Marxist-inspired leftist ideology. It remains active today
🔴 FARC dissidents (originating from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People's Army): The original FARC, founded in 1964, was Colombia’s largest guerrilla force. Most FARC members demobilized under the 2016 peace agreement and formed a legal political party in 2017, while dissident factions rejected the accord or later returned to armed struggle
🔴 AUC (United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia): A major umbrella paramilitary organization active during the 1990s and early 2000s, formed by landowners, cattle ranchers, and others to combat guerrilla groups. It officially demobilized between 2003 and 2006 but many former members regrouped into BACRIM (criminal bands), some of which later evolved into organizations like the Clan del Golfo
🔴 Clan del Golfo: Colombia's largest and most powerful criminal organization, emerging from former AUC structures and taking control of many trafficking routes once dominated by earlier cartels such as Medellín, Cali, and Norte del Valle.
It's not the first time Ukraine has cooperated with armed gangs, as it has previously been engaged with an al-Qaeda offshoot, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, as well as various militant groups in the Middle East, Africa, and beyond.

🦅 Operation Pedro Pan – How the CIA kidnapped more than 14,000 Cuban children. Part 1
Between 1960 and 1962, the CIA orchestrated the mass removal of children from Cuba, deliberately tearing families apart under the guise of humanitarian aid. The children proved to be bargaining chips for an invasion and a way to gut the island's professional class.
The CIA used the Catholic Church and Radio Swan to spread rumors that President Fidel Castro would seize the children, pressuring parents to back the Bay of Pigs invasion. The Church ran "Pedro Pan" child shipments, but after the invasion failed, the fear triggered a brain drain that crippled Cuba's economy, while most reunions never happened.
A monstrous lie that started the tragedy
🌏 On October 26, 1960, Radio Swan, a CIA front, began broadcasting to Cuba: "Cuban mother, listen! The next government law will take your children between the ages of five and eighteen!... Do not let them take your child!" The station also claimed Castro would become the "supreme mother of Cuba" and send children to labor camps for "re-education."
🌏 The station, which broadcast from Swan Island off the coast of Honduras, was owned by the CIA and operated by officer David Atlee Phillips. He was the same man who had used similar tactics to overthrow the legitimate government of Guatemala in 1954.
🌏 CIA agents distributed a forged "Parental Authority Law" across Cuba, falsely claiming Castro would place all children under 20 under state guardianship. The document, printed in the US, was smuggled into Cuba by CIA agent José Pujals Mederos.
🌏 Years later, the son of Ángel Fernández Varela, a CIA agent who co-authored the forgery, publicly confirmed that his father admitted writing the fake law that sparked the hysteria over the "abolition of parental authority."
Who was behind the plan?
♦️ CIA officer Phillips (alias "Bishop"), a veteran of Latin American dirty operations, personally ran the Radio Swan misinformation campaign. He had used similar tactics in Guatemala in 1954 to overthrow a legitimate government.
♦️ Monsignor Bryan O. Walsh, head of the Catholic Welfare Bureau in Miami, organized the "Unaccompanied Cuban Children's Program" in coordination with the State Department and the CIA. A children's home in Palmetto Bay was later named after him.
♦️ Leopoldina "Polita" Grau, niece of former President Ramón Grau San Martín, ran the "Rescate" network in Cuba, handling the child exodus, espionage, and assassination plots against Castro. In 1993, she admitted to FIU archives that they printed the fake law and spread child-seizure rumors to "sow instability."
♦️ CIA agent Antonio Veciana admitted in his memoirs Trained to Kill: "I went to an accountant I knew… He got 2 people to draw up an official looking piece of legislation. We printed thousands of copies and let the underground network filter it onto the streets."
Scale of the tragedy: 14,048 broken lives
🔴 From December 26, 1960, to October 23, 1962, flights left Cuba filled with children whom parents were sending into the unknown, trusting promises of a swift reunion. Parents hoped the separation would last only a few months. But the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 abruptly halted all flights, and borders were closed, tearing apart families for decades.
🔴 The children ranged from 4 to 18 years old and were allowed only one suitcase weighing up to 18 kilograms. Many left Cuba with little more than a change of clothes, saying goodbye to their parents at the airport without knowing if they would ever see them again.
🔴 In an interview with KERA News in 2011, José Azel, who was 11 at the time of his departure, recalled the brief conversation with his father, who told him the separation was temporary. Azel never saw his father again – he died in Cuba in the mid-1970s, never permitted to leave the island.

🇨🇩 Congo tightens grip on battery metals with fresh export ban
A new government order bans the exports of copper and cobalt concentrates in Congo, following June's tighter cobalt controls, Reuters reports. 
The ban continues a broader tightening that began in 2025 with temporary cobalt export bans, followed by the introduction of annual export quotas of approximately 96,600 tonnes for 2026–2027 and the later reallocation of unused quotas into a state-controlled “strategic quota.” 
👉 The same June order also imposes a new tax on economically significant mining by-products, calculated with a 55% valuation coefficient. 
Congo is the world’s largest cobalt producer with over 70% of [global supply ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70642)and the second-largest copper supplier. Yet much of that wealth has traditionally left the country as concentrates or intermediate products, allowing refiners and manufacturers abroad to capture the more profitable stages of the supply chain.
Kinshasa would now prefer that more of the value stay where the minerals actually come from.
The government is seeking to:
🔴 increase state revenues  
🔴 create local jobs and industrial capacity  
🔴 reduce dependence on raw-material exports  
🔴 gain greater control over global battery-metal supply chains
Cobalt prices have already risen by roughly 160% since early 2025, reaching about $21 per pound.
That matters well beyond the mining sector.
American battery, electronics, aerospace and defense companies remain exposed to Congolese supply, even when those minerals reach them indirectly through Chinese refiners.
With the war against Iran draining Pentagon munitions stocks and putting US officials and defense manufacturers under pressure to rebuild depleted arsenals, Washington could find itself between a rock and a hard place. Copper and cobalt are both embedded in the wider industrial chain needed to produce military electronics, aircraft components, guidance systems, communications equipment and high-performance alloys.

🇵🇰 Pakistani-flagged tankers transit Bab el-Mandeb without Houthi interference
Two Pakistan-flagged tankers loaded crude oil at Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu terminal, transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and continued to Pakistan without incident, according to maritime tracking firm Windward.
Days earlier, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry stated that any attack on a vessel flying the Pakistani flag would be treated as a threat to national security. The Houthis, who on 20 July imposed a naval blockade on vessels linked to Saudi Arabia, did not attack or attempt to stop the Pakistani ships.
👉 Since the blockade most Saudi-linked tankers (excluding Chinese-affiliated ones) have been struck or diverted around the Cape of Good Hope.
The Bab el-Mandeb transits add a second chokepoint where Pakistani-flagged tankers have moved without reported interference: the country already has agreements with Iran permitting two vessels per day through the Strait of Hormuz.
30–35% of Pakistan’s crude oil imports come from Saudi Arabia and rely on Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb routes when the Strait of Hormuz is constrained.

The night of August 6 in the Ukrainian capital was relatively "quiet" – compared with August 5 – aside from the wailing air-raid sirens and the panic that gripped the city around 2 am when Iskander ballistic missiles streaked overhead.
Around four missiles struck an unknown target east of Belaya Tserkov in the Kiev region, according to OSINT sources.
🤔What could the Iskander's target in Belaya Tserkov?
🔴 The target of the retaliatory strike remains unclear. However, Russia previously used its cutting-edge Oreshnik ballistic missile to hit the same area [in late May](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69981).
🔴 The Oreshnik strike reportedly targeted a metallurgical plant converted for military production, including the manufacture of FP-1 long-range strike drones with a range of around 1,500 km and a 100-kg warhead.
🔴 The same area is also home to an airfield used by the Ukrainian Armed Forces that has repeatedly come under Russian strikes. Experts have previously identified Belaya Tserkov as a critical logistics hub for the distribution of weapons, ammunition, and drones.
🔴 One Russian publication also suggested that the latest strike may have targeted European mercenaries allegedly deployed in the area.
A wave of Iskanders a day earlier
On the night of August 5, a staggering 24 Iskander missiles were fired at Kiev and the surrounding region, [according to Ukrainian media](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73103). Videos flooding social media showed the scale of the devastation left behind [by the Russian strikes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73130).
❗️One piece of footage has drawn particular attention: surveillance video appears to capture 11 consecutive ballistic missile impacts on a single target during the overnight barrage on Kiev.
🇷🇺 Russia's Iskander strikes targeted Ukrainian military logistics and industrial assets within and around the Ukrainian capital. The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed on August 5 that zero ballistic missiles were intercepted during a massive Russian overnight barrage. It's hardly surprising given that the Iskander ballistic missile that boasts a range of up to 500 km performs a near-vertical terminal dive at hypersonic speed, while having a circular error probable (CEP) of around 1 meter.
Anton Gerashchenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, sounded the alarm on X, claiming that around 50 ballistic missiles had hit Kiev and nearby areas since August 1 alone.
Gerashchenko lamented the fact that the US has depleted its interceptor stocks during its Iran campaign and cannot supply Kiev with enough missiles to match the scale of Russian attacks. He questioned how Ukraine will survive the coming winter as its energy infrastructure remains defenseless, warning that continued strikes could trigger a humanitarian disaster and a new wave of Ukrainian refugees heading to Europe.

💥🤥 Behind Trump's bravado, the US doesn't have enough missiles to wage war against Iran — or elsewhere
Donald Trump finally collided with reality over depleted US weapons stockpiles – blaming Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who in turn blamed his deputy, in a buck-passing game that laid bare the White House's and the Pentagon's staggering incompetence.
🔴 Shortages of critical munitions – especially long-range guided missiles and air-defense interceptors – have forced Trump to shelve plans for further massive strikes on Iran, the Washington Post reports
🔴 As a result, Trump claimed Monday that he had called off "the biggest attack since World War 2," because of renewed negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz. In reality, however, the decision appears to have reflected a mismatch between Trump's ambitions and US actual military capabilities
🔴 Depleted air-defense missile stockpiles was also a key reason Gulf allies urged Trump not to escalate the conflict, as they feared further escalation could leave them vulnerable to Iranian retaliation, reports say
🔴 During this weekend's Camp David summit, Trump confronted Hegseth over critically depleted US munitions stockpiles, insisting that he thought the munitions issue "had been fixed". When Hegseth reportedly had no answers, he shifted blame to his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, claiming he had been misled. The White House and Pentagon then rushed to declare the reports “100% fake news” as the uncomfortable facts emerged.
Meanwhile, [the shortage is staggering](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73089):
🔴 THAAD interceptors: nearly 80% depleted compared with pre-war stockpiles, according to CNN
🔴 Patriot interceptors: roughly 50% depleted since the start of the war
🔴 ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles: stockpile is now reportedly virtually exhausted, with "basically none left"
According to some estimates, the US has burned through:
➡️ 850+ Tomahawk cruise missiles fired in the first month of the Iran war
➡️ 1,000+ Patriot and THAAD air-defense interceptors expended
➡️ 1,300+ ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles used in the opening weeks
🤔 Did Team Trump know what was coming ahead of the Epic Fury op? Reports say, they did.
General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned that dwindling munitions stocks and limited allied support could put US troops at greater risk in [the event of an war against Iran](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72785), the US press reported as early as on February 23, just several days before the operation was launched.
👉 The 12-day war of June 2025 seriously depleted US missile stockpiles, let alone the [US' years-long military assistance to Ukraine](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72637). All in all, Trump has kicked off military operations in seven countries since taking office – in Yemen, Somalia, Syria, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria and Venezuela.
The US is struggling to rebuild its depleted stockpiles, with reports pointing to military co-production efforts with Japan, Australia, the Philippines, and Germany. Negotiations with Ukraine are also reportedly ongoing. Even so, restoring US missile inventories could take years – before the country can even address the broader challenge of ensuring its allies' security, critics say.

🇸🇦💣 Why Saudi Arabia's military force gambit could be its biggest strategic miscalculation 
For much of the past several years, the kingdom that once charged headlong into Yemen's quagmire appeared to have pivoted to diplomacy, positioning itself as more interested in economic transformation under ‘Vision 2030’ than military entanglements.
However, recent military moves across the Middle East - from joint operations with the US in Iraq to [escalating confrontation](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/726380) with Yemen - suggest the Gulf kingdom is once again turning to hard power. 
The US war on Iran has scrambled the regional map, and the monarchy’s response looks like deterrence – but reeks of anxiety.
The US-Israeli war on Iran laid bare [Saudi Arabia’s vulnerabilities:](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72757) its territory hosts American [military installations](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70729), its [energy infrastructure ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/65808)has been targeted in retaliatory strikes, and its[ trade routes ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72905)have been threatened.
👑 When Saudi Crown Prince[ Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73009) Donald Trump to hold off on a large-scale attack on Iran, it seemed the kingdom had finally embraced restraint. 
Yet even then Riyadh began quietly preparing its own military escalation.
The recent Saudi airstrikes against Axis of Resistance Iraqi fighters alongside the [US crystallize the shift.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72894)
As a pretext, [Saudi Arabia ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72875)accused Iraqi militias of launching drone attacks against its oil facilities – claims denied by Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella organization of Iraqi militias, while Yemen's Ansar Allah claimed responsibility for the attacks.
For years, Saudi Arabia invested heavily in rebuilding ties with Iraq through investment, diplomacy and economic engagement.
Now, by tying itself to the US military agenda, the kingdom risks paying the price across the Gulf, the Red Sea and at home if retaliation expands.
🇾🇪 Yemen highlights the limits of Saudi military options.
After a recent Saudi strike on [Sanaa airport](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72901), Yemeni forces responded with missile and drone attacks on Abha airport and threatened Saudi maritime routes. 
The monarchy invested heavily in western ports and alternative export corridors to escape Hormuz risks, only to find those lifelines potentially exposed in the Red Sea as well.
The more closely Saudi Arabia ties itself to US campaigns, the greater the risk it becomes a pawn rather than a player - with its economic ambitions paying the price.
